performers: Skidmore College Orchestra, per the Free Music Archive and Internet Archive; not named on the Commons page
intro: Hartmann’s gate never rises in Kyiv, but Mussorgsky builds it in E♭ major. Brass, a chant and pealing bells turn the last picture into a public ceremony.

sections.label: A · The brass gate in E♭ major
sections.mNote: Broad chords, marked majestic and grand

sections.label: B · A chant in A♭ minor
sections.mNote: Plain chordal phrases replace the broad brass tune

sections.label: A′ · The gate above running scales
sections.mNote: The E♭ major theme returns amid flowing octaves

sections.label: B′ · The chant in E♭ minor
sections.mNote: The hymn returns a fifth higher

sections.label: C · Bells gather around the Promenade
sections.mNote: Low tolling notes grow into overlapping bell figures

sections.label: A″ · The gate theme strides more slowly
sections.mNote: Meno mosso: the melody broadens above three-part beats

sections.label: A‴ · The final E♭ proclamation

cues.title: The gate in brass
cues.text: The brass open in E♭ major with a tune built to carry across a square. Mussorgsky’s directions are Maestoso and Con grandezza — majestic, with grandeur. Broad chords hold the melody up while softer woodwinds answer.
cues.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, opening bars; orchestration: Joanna Wyld, Philharmonia listening guide, 7 April 2022, p. 7: https://philharmonia-assets.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/2022/04/07.04.22_RFH-online.pdf. Ravel attribution for this recording remains inferred.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A helmet above the gate
cues.text: Hartmann’s design has tinted brick, an imperial eagle and a three-storey belfry with a cupola shaped like a Slavic helmet. The planned stone gates of Kyiv remain on paper. Mussorgsky supplies the bells.
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg describes the unbuilt design and its belfry: https://www.bso.org/works/pictures-at-an-exhibition. The bell writing is discussed by Orrin Howard: https://www.laphil.com/works/pictures-at-an-exhibition-modest-mussorgsky-zs2phpn9

cues.title: Scales around the brass
cues.text: The gate theme returns in E♭ major. Strings and woodwinds pour scales around the broad brass melody, moving up and down while the tune keeps its stately pace.
cues.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 47–63; strings and wind runs around the brass melody: Joanna Wyld, Philharmonia listening guide, p. 7.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Ravel’s Paris première
cues.text: In the summer of 1922, Ravel turns Mussorgsky’s piano suite into an orchestral score for Serge Koussevitzky. Koussevitzky conducts it in Paris on 22 October. In 1930 he records it with the Boston Symphony Orchestra.
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg gives the commission, 22 October 1922 Paris première and 1930 Boston recording: https://www.bso.org/works/pictures-at-an-exhibition

cues.title: The walker among the bells
cues.text: The Promenade returns amid the bell figures. The tune that first belonged to one trumpet now sounds inside the finale’s great gathering. Above and below it, quick notes keep the bells ringing.
cues.evidence: Peter Laki identifies the late Promenade return: https://www.clevelandorchestra.com/works/pictures-at-an-exhibition-mussorgsky. Lamm’s piano edition, bars 97–110, places it within the bell passage.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The gate takes larger steps
cues.text: The main theme broadens at Meno mosso, sempre maestoso — slower, still majestic. Its chords now sound against groups of three half-notes. The bass and upper parts answer across several octaves.
cues.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 114–135, Meno mosso and minim triplets: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/ftp/MussorgskyM/pictures-at-an-exhibition/pictures-at-an-exhibition-lys/great-gate-meno.ily
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The bass moves underfoot
cues.text: Repeated chords keep ringing while the bass moves from A♭ to B♭ and C♭. The same three-part pulse continues through each change of harmony. The chords start to swell again.
cues.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 136–155: minim triplets, A♭–B♭–C♭ bass and crescendo; Mutopia transcription.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: E♭ from top to bottom
cues.text: The last proclamation grows broader still: Grave, sempre allargando. Low E♭ supports the great chords, and the final pages stretch across the whole range of the orchestra. The suite ends on E♭.
cues.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 162–173, Grave, sempre allargando and final E♭ octaves; Mutopia transcription. Ravel’s full orchestral ending is described in Joanna Wyld’s Philharmonia guide.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A♭ minor inside the gate
transitions.from: A · The brass gate in E♭ major
transitions.to: B · A chant in A♭ minor
transitions.how: The broad E♭ major statement ends, and an A♭ minor chord begins the chant. The score marks it senza espressione, without expression: plain notes moving together. Ravel exchanges the brass-led tune for quieter woodwinds.
transitions.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 29–46: A♭ minor chant and senza espressione; woodwind contrast: Joanna Wyld, Philharmonia listening guide, p. 7.

transitions.title: E♭ major returns with running octaves
transitions.from: B · A chant in A♭ minor
transitions.to: A′ · The gate above running scales
transitions.how: The chant ends on the bare fifth A♭–E♭. E♭ major returns forcefully beneath a descending scale, marked energico. Ravel keeps the main tune in brass while strings and woodwinds race around it.
transitions.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 45–55; orchestration: Joanna Wyld, Philharmonia listening guide, p. 7.

transitions.title: The chant returns a fifth higher
transitions.from: A′ · The gate above running scales
transitions.to: B′ · The chant in E♭ minor
transitions.how: The running octaves climb to B♭ and stop. The chant begins again, now in E♭ minor, a fifth above its first appearance. The long notes and senza espressione marking remain, with G♭ in place of the gate theme’s G♮.
transitions.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 63–80: ascent to B♭ and E♭ minor transposition of the chant, marked senza espressione; Mutopia transcription.

transitions.title: Low bells start to overlap
transitions.from: B′ · The chant in E♭ minor
transitions.to: C · Bells gather around the Promenade
transitions.how: The hymn ends on E♭ and B♭. Low A♭ and C♭ now alternate beneath tolling upper notes. Triplets enter, then quavers: the bell figures overlap more closely as the music gathers towards the Promenade.
transitions.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 79–97: bare fifth, alternating A♭/C♭ bass and progressively shorter note values. Orrin Howard’s LA Phil note describes the bells.

transitions.title: The scales stop; the gate broadens
transitions.from: C · Bells gather around the Promenade
transitions.to: A″ · The gate theme strides more slowly
transitions.how: A descending scale runs to low C and stops under a fermata. Meno mosso, sempre maestoso brings the gate theme back in E♭ major. Its first chord has G in the bass; broad triplets now carry the melody across the orchestra.
transitions.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 111–120: descending scale to C, fermata and Meno mosso return over G; Mutopia transcription.

transitions.title: A♭ starts the final climb
transitions.from: A″ · The gate theme strides more slowly
transitions.to: D · Repeated chords above a moving bass
transitions.how: The gate theme settles on E♭. The bass then moves to A♭ beneath an F minor seventh chord, repeated in broad triplets. B♭ and C♭ follow in the bass as the chords keep ringing; a crescendo starts the final climb.
transitions.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 134–155: E♭ close, F–A♭–C–E♭ chord over A♭, moving bass and crescendo; Mutopia transcription.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Skidmore College Orchestra (orchestra, as stated by the Free Music Archive; conductor unknown)
fields.note: The Commons page names no performer (“see Musopen for performance author information”). The Free Music Archive album of 15 tracks by the Skidmore College Orchestra lists a track of the same title and length (5:29; this file is 5:28), and the Internet Archive item for the first Promenade credits the same orchestra. The identification of this file with that track rests on title and length; the Musopen performer page was not opened. Conductor: unknown.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Orchestral performance; Ravel’s 1922 orchestration is the probable version but is not named by any source
fields.note: Neither Commons, the Free Music Archive nor the Internet Archive names the orchestrator. The album’s four Promenades (none between “Samuel Goldenberg and Schmuÿle” and Limoges) match Ravel’s layout, and a 2015 Commons talk-page comment calls the recording Ravel’s orchestration of a rather poor Skidmore performance. The commenter gives no source. Instrument names in the listening notes follow Ravel’s scoring conditionally, as the introduction says; the audio report does not identify instruments.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: No session date is documented. The Internet Archive item says “date unknown, 2008 at the latest”; the Free Music Archive lists the album as released 6 April 2009; this file was uploaded to Commons on 2008-01-21. None of these is a recording date.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: No venue is documented. The Free Music Archive biography describes the orchestra as a semi-professional ensemble of Skidmore students and regional professionals; this is not a recording location.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: The original release is not identified; Musopen and the Free Music Archive are distribution channels.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Mussorgsky’s piano suite (he died in 1881) is public domain; Commons marks the music PD-old-100. An orchestration is a separate work with its own term and is not cleared here.
fields.note: The Commons notice covers Mussorgsky’s music only. If the version is Ravel’s, his orchestration is not assessed in this dossier.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 1 — recording release: PD-author public-domain dedication by Musopen, with Wikimedia VRTS permission ticket 2008012110017088.
fields.note: The file description applies PD-author|Musopen to the recording separately from PD-old-100 for the music, and cites the VRTS ticket; the page is in “Items with VRTS permission confirmed”. Musopen’s reproduced policy says the music is public domain with no restrictions; its requests not to sell the recordings and to credit Musopen are courtesy requests, not a non-commercial licence. The Internet Archive copy of the first Promenade is marked CC0 1.0. Session date is not needed for this route.

composer.epithet: He could make a singer sound like a frightened child, a drunken monk or a tsar who can no longer bear his own thoughts.
facts: Piano with Anton Gerke; composition with Mily Balakirev, outside the conservatory
Guards officer until 1858; later a clerk in the Forestry Department and Government Control
Borodin, Cui, Balakirev, Rimsky-Korsakov; Vladimir Stasov and Viktor Hartmann
Boris Godunov, unfinished operas, three song cycles, Pictures at an Exhibition
composer.background:
When Borodin met Mussorgsky at a Saint Petersburg military hospital in 1856, the seventeen-year-old officer was immaculate: close-fitting uniform, polished manners, well-kept hands. He played extracts from Il trovatore and La traviata at the piano while admirers gathered round. Twenty-five years later another hospital would provide his most familiar likeness: Repin’s painting of a man in a dressing gown, hair in disorder, eyes still alert. There is a great deal of music between those two rooms.

Mussorgsky was born at Karevo on his family’s estate. His mother taught him the piano; his nurse’s stories stirred the improvisations he remembered from childhood. At ten he went to school in Saint Petersburg and studied piano with Anton Gerke. The School of Guards Cadets followed in 1852, then a commission in the Preobrazhensky Regiment in 1856. His father paid to publish his first piano piece, a polka. The boy could play for a drawing room before he knew how an orchestra worked.
